title: Broker Use Case Analysis
description: Match real-world messaging patterns to the broker that handles them best.

data.text: Broker selection becomes much easier when you start from the problem, not the product. Every messaging scenario has a natural shape: request-reply, fan-out, event sourcing, or background task processing. Each shape stresses different broker capabilities.

Point-to-point messaging, where one producer sends to one consumer, is the simplest pattern. It works equally well with RabbitMQ, Kafka, or SQS. Fan-out, where one event must reach many subscribers, is where brokers diverge. RabbitMQ uses exchanges to route copies to multiple queues. Kafka relies on consumer groups reading the same topic. SQS does not natively fan out—you must combine it with SNS or use EventBridge.

An e-commerce system places an order, charges a card, updates inventory, and sends a confirmation email. Each step must complete reliably, but they do not need to happen in parallel. A work queue pattern fits here: one consumer type processes each stage in sequence.

data.title: Recommended Broker
data.text: RabbitMQ is ideal for this pipeline. Its direct exchange routes orders to a single processing queue, and dead-letter exchanges capture failed orders for manual review.

A streaming analytics pipeline ingests clickstream events, enriches them, and writes aggregated metrics to a dashboard. The volume is high, and multiple analytics jobs need to consume the same raw stream independently.

data.title: Kafka consumer group in C#
Recommended Broker
data.text: Kafka is the natural choice. Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic without competing, and long retention lets you re-process historical data after a bug fix.
A web application needs to offload email sending, image resizing, and report generation so the request thread is not blocked. Jobs should be retried on failure and expire after a deadline.

data.title: SQS message with visibility timeout (Node.js SDK)
Recommended Broker
data.text: SQS is excellent for this scenario. Visibility timeout handles retries automatically, and dead-letter queues capture jobs that exceed the retry limit without extra code.

cards.title: RabbitMQ
cards.description: Best for request-reply, complex routing, and low-latency work queues where message ordering per queue matters.

cards.title: Kafka
cards.description: Best for event streaming, log aggregation, and analytics pipelines that need replay and high throughput.

cards.title: SQS
cards.description: Best for background jobs and decoupling microservices on AWS with zero infrastructure to manage.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Match the broker to the pattern, not the pattern to the broker.
RabbitMQ shines for routing-heavy, low-latency pipelines.
Kafka shines for streaming, replay, and multi-consumer analytics.
SQS shines for simple background jobs on AWS with zero ops.
One architecture can use multiple brokers—do not force a single tool across every problem.
data.takeaway: Use case analysis is the fastest way to cut through broker marketing and find the right fit for your specific problem.
